toc.title: Freeze is not burnout, depression, or shutdown
What it looks like from the inside
What helps, and in what order
A small practice to start now

blocks.p: You're getting things done. You're showing up, you're answering texts, you're making dinner. But underneath all of it, you feel activated, but flat and far away, like you're watching your own life through a foot of glass. That's functional freeze. Let's walk through what it is, why it's there, and some real, small ways to start coming out of it.

Let's start with what freeze is, because I see it getting mixed up out there. Freeze is not its own separate, distinct autonomic state. Freeze is a mixed autonomic state. A mixed state is what you get when two of your primary autonomic states are running at the same time.

There are three of them. Play is safety plus mobilization. Stillness is safety plus shutdown. And freeze is mobilization plus immobilization, or flight or fight plus shutdown. They're both active at the same time.

So freeze combines mobility and immobility. It's like having the gas pedal and the brake pressed at the same time. There's mobilization running, and that's the gas: your sympathetic branch revving you up, ready to act. And there's shutdown running at the same time, and that's the brake: your dorsal vagal branch pulling you toward immobility and numbness and disconnection and feeling drained. Both of those at once. That's what freeze is.

So what does the word functional add? It describes the severity, not a different state. Functional just means you can still get through your day while you're in freeze. A functional freeze can be mild, like tension, but manageable. Or it can be severe, with chronic panic, overwhelm, rage, or fear running just underneath everything that you do.
Same state, just a different intensity.

blocks.h: Freeze is not burnout, depression, or shutdown

blocks.p: Let me quickly separate functional freeze from a few things it gets confused with, because the mix-up can send people toward the wrong kind of help, and we need clarity here. Functional freeze is different from, but connected to, burnout, depression, and shutdown.

Burnout is depletion. It's running on empty over time, and it might be the result of a functional freeze. That's something I hear from my clients pretty often. You manage and manage and manage the freeze, crash into burnout, then recover just enough, and then you go right back into your freeze baseline and do it again.

Depression is a clinical diagnosis: low mood, low energy, low motivation, most days, for weeks, maybe months and longer. Through the polyvagal lens, the underlying mechanism is dorsal shutdown. It's a biological mechanism.

The third one is shutdown. Shutdown and freeze are not the same thing. Shutdown is collapse. It's the brake without the gas. It's the numb and disconnected. Freeze is the brake and the gas together. People cycle between the two: freeze while they're managing, and then shutdown when they crash.

Shutdown is a part of freeze, but shutdown is its own thing as well. So they're different states, and that matters, because what actually helps them is slightly different, though overlapping. I don't think burnout and shutdown are necessarily the same thing either, but those two might be connected as well.

blocks.h: What it looks like from the inside

blocks.p: Picture a normal Tuesday. Your inbox is handled. Good job, by the way. Your kids are picked up. That's important. Good job. And a quick "Good, how you doing?" to your neighbor.

But inside, you can't taste your food. Something funny happens in a group chat, and you just stare at it. You overthink your reply, and then you move on without replying at all. There's this low hum of "I should be doing more," but it never actually turns into doing more. You might be smiling on the outside, but internally you're wired and far away.
You're not broken. Hopefully you know that. Your gas and your brake are both on. Stuck, not broken.
These signs tend to cluster:

ul: On edge for no clear reason.
Feeling far from people, even the ones you love.
Panic or rage or overwhelm or fear as an undercurrent underneath it all.
Breath that stays tight and shallow in your chest.

blocks.p: It's a revolving door of tension and collapse. It gets hard to start things, and hard to care about the things you normally care about, or to act on them.

Your nervous system has one very old, simple job: keep you protected and alive. When something feels like too much, it shifts into defense. Fight or flight is the mobilized one, the gas. But when fight or flight isn't possible, when you can't run and you can't fight, the body reaches for an older defense and slams on the brake. That's shutdown.
Freeze is what you get when the brake of shutdown comes on but the flight or fight gas is still pressed. So it's not a malfunction. It's protection doing exactly what it evolved to do.

Freeze evolved to be temporary. It's like going immobile as a danger passes by, or bracing for impact: coiling up like a spring and then releasing when it's possible to release. The trouble is that we humans tend to get stuck in freeze. Stuck, not broken. And that's where the benefit of freeze gets lost, and life gets a lot harder.
So what do you do about it? First, what not to do, because the two obvious options can backfire.

The first is to push through it. Yes, you can push to get through a meeting, but pushing takes whatever gas you have all the way down to E. Pushing may be needed to deal with life, and that's fine. But it doesn't deal with the underlying stuckness of freeze. Push long enough and you can tip yourself over into full shutdown.

The second is to check out and do nothing. You might call it rest, and rest does matter for freeze. It's very important. But it depends on how. Not all rest is equal. Collapsing on the couch and disappearing into a screen for six hours is not actual rest. That doesn't count. We'll call that faux rest. And faux rest tends to deepen the problem, setting up a loop: you faux rest, feel worse, ignore your problems, faux rest some more, feel worse, and on and on.
The rest that actually helps is the kind where you're present within it, mindful of the moment you're actually in.

blocks.h: What helps, and in what order

blocks.p: So if it's not pushing harder and it's not checking out into faux rest, what is it? It runs in a specific order, and it depends on how much access you have to safety.

Safety has to thaw the freeze first. When your body picks up enough small safety signals, the brake of shutdown, that immobility, can come off. And once the immobility lifts, the mobilization that was frozen underneath can finally start to move instead of just sitting there stuck. Safety thaws the freeze. The brake releases, and then the stuck flight or fight energy can move through and out.
But your safety has to hold while that happens, which means it has to get stronger. Which means this is not a one-time fix. It happens in small doses, over time, with patience.

blocks.h: A small practice to start now

blocks.p: Here's one small way to start now. It's a quick orienting and small movement exercise. Don't worry about doing it perfectly. Just follow along.
You can start wherever you are and however you are. There's no right way to sit or stand. You can sit, stand, lie down, or walk if you want to. It doesn't matter.

Let your eyes go where they want to go. Don't direct them. Just let them drift, and follow them. As they move, or don't, notice a few things. Notice something that's moving, like a leaf on a branch, or shadows from the tree outside swaying on the wall. Notice which colors your eyes are drawn to. Notice light and dark. Stay with that for thirty seconds, or longer if you want to.
Then take one bigger breath in on purpose, and let it out slowly if it's comfortable. Don't force it. Let your next couple of breaths happen on their own. Don't control them. Just be with them.
Then briefly acknowledge the freeze you have underneath it all. If you have the capacity, feel it directly at a very low level, and keep that part pretty short.
After that, do one small movement. Wiggle your toes. Make a fist and release it. Roll your wrists, or your ankles, or your shoulders. Then tell yourself, "Good job."
Let your eyes wander one more time, and take one more intentional breath in and out to finish. That's it.

It's a really simple little practice, and something you could do on your own for a minute every day. Letting your eyes lead and be drawn to what they like is a cue of safety. The small movement is gentle mobilization. You're not trying to feel amazing. You're giving the brake permission to come off a couple of millimeters, and then letting a little of the stuck energy potentially start to move.

blocks.why: This article is about practicing. This is the practice built from your check-ins.

blocks.p: That little practice will not cure your freeze, and I'm not going to pretend it will, especially if you're new to these types of practices. What it does, in small doses over time, is build the foundation: a little more safety, a little more presence, and maybe a little less defense.

Over time, with reps like that, you might notice small signs of your system letting go. A shiver or a tingle moving through you. A bigger breath that arrives on its own. A yawn. Those are good. That's regulation happening spontaneously, not forced.
Functional freeze is common and workable, and for a lot of people, small daily practices plus real, mindful rest are enough to start shifting it. Of course, seek a professional if it's severe.

Freeze is not a character flaw. It's not a failure, and it's not brokenness. It's your gas and your brake both on at the same time, for reasons that once made complete sense. You're not broken, you're stuck.
And stuckness can move. It's not permanent.
